# Hosting a GitHub Page - R Cheat Sheet


For this exercise, you will create a sample web page and then host it on your GitHub page.

## Styled Text

At the core, QMD files are text files, and they allow you to use a very lightweight "markup" language to style text, similar to html, but much less fussy.

Outside of the codeblocks (the gray sections where we write code), we can style any text using standard markdown styling.

This is a nice guide to styling text with markdown: [Markdown guide](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html)

We can create headings similar to html's h1 to h6 with hashtags.

##### This is an h5

We can create links, like this: [google](https://google.com)

We can **bold** or *italic* text.

We can create bulleted lists.

-   bullet one
-   bullet two
-   bullet three

## Code blocks

We can also add special code inside of code blocks -- the gray sections where we write code -- that control how they render in our html document. These output options let us do things like:

-   Show or hide the code when we render our html document (echo: true or false)
-   Prevent the code from actually running when we render our html document (eval: true or false)
-   Hide warnings from outputing when we render our html document (warning: true or false)

There's a [full guide here](https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html#output-options).

The code below, for example, will output the text inside the print statement when rendered to html, but the actual code -- the print() function -- will be hidden.

## Create your website

In place of these instructions, you will paste your project one paragraph story idea into this document and any code you've developed so far.

You will need to load libraries and data because rendering a page requires a full R session to execute on the code.

First, create H1 headers

**For example:**

# Income and Vacancies of Baltimore Neighborhoods 2020

## Looking at wealth inequality in Charm City

```{r eval=FALSE, include=TRUE}

# You will write your code in chunks but not execute the data. Use {r eval=FALSE, include=TRUE} in the header so the page will render without running the actual code.
income_vacancy %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = community)) +
  geom_point(aes(y=income_2020), color = "#64D197", stroke=5) +
  geom_point(aes(y=vacant_2020*1000), stroke=5, color = "#FB8AE3") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "2020 Income (Green)", limits=c(0, 62000), labels=scales::dollar_format(),
    sec.axis = sec_axis(~./60000, name="2020 Percent Vacancies (Red)", labels = scales::percent))+
  #scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Income and Vacancies of Baltimore Neighborhoods 2020",
    x = "Community",
    caption = "source: BNIA Data - By: Parker Leipzig and Rob Wells"
  )
```

## Set up for hosting

- Create a new folder in your repository called `docs` (if one isn't there already).
- Rename your Quarto document to `index.qmd`.
- Move `index.qmd` into the `docs` folder. *(Note: If your code loads any local data or images, you will need to update their file paths to start with `../`, e.g., `../data.csv`.)*

## Render this document as an HTML page

- Make sure `index.qmd` is open from inside the `docs` folder.
- Click the **Render** button. This will create `index.html` (and a supporting `index_files` folder) inside `docs`.
- Open **GitHub Desktop**. Make sure all new and modified files inside `docs` (both `index.html` and `index_files`) are checked.
- Write a commit message, click **Commit to main**, and click **Push origin**.

## Turn on GitHub Pages

- Go to your repository on GitHub in your web browser (e.g., `https://github.com/djnf-data-2026/xxxx`).
- Click **Settings** in the top repository menu bar.
- In the left sidebar, click **Pages**.
- Under **Build and deployment > Branch**:
  1. Change the first dropdown from **None** to **main**.
  2. Change the second dropdown from **/ (root)** to **/docs**.
  3. Click **Save**.

## View your live site

- Wait 1–2 minutes for GitHub to build your page, then refresh the **Settings > Pages** page.
- At the top, you should see a box saying: **"Your site is live at `https://djnf-data-2026.github.io/xxxx/`"**
- Click that link to view your hosted page.
-   If it works, email it to robwells\@umd.edu


## Troubleshooting

- **"404 File not found" error:**
  - Make sure your repository is set to public. Settings | General --> scroll down to "Danger Zone" at the end and your repository is set for `This repository is currently public.`
  - Make sure your rendered file is named `index.html` (all lowercase) and is located **inside** the `docs` folder—not in the main repository folder.
  -Make sure the folder is `docs` (all lowercase) and is located in the main repository (root) folder.
  -Make sure the R code is `index.qmd`
  - Double-check that you pushed your changes in GitHub Desktop (look at your repo on GitHub.com to verify `docs/index.html` is visible there).
  - Verify that **Settings > Pages** is set to **main** and **/docs** (and that you clicked **Save**).

- **My page loads, but looks like plain text with missing charts or styling:**
  - You likely pushed `index.html` without the supporting `index_files` folder. Open GitHub Desktop, check any remaining files inside `docs/index_files`, commit them, and click **Push origin**.
  - *(Alternative fix)* Add `embed-resources: true` under `format: html:` in your `index.qmd` YAML header, re-render, and push the updated `index.html`. I have added this change to the header on this document.

- **The "Your site is live" banner hasn't appeared yet, or my recent edits aren't showing up:**
  - GitHub Pages usually takes **1–2 minutes** to rebuild after a push. Wait a moment and do a hard refresh in your browser (**Cmd + Shift + R** on Mac, **Ctrl + Shift + R** on Windows).
  - You can check build progress by clicking the **Actions** tab in your GitHub repository—a yellow dot means it is still building, a green checkmark means it is live, and a red X means the build failed.

```{=html}
<script type="text/javascript">!function(){"use strict";window.addEventListener("message",(function(a){if(void 0!==a.data["datawrapper-height"]){var e=document.querySelectorAll("iframe");for(var t in a.data["datawrapper-height"])for(var r=0;r<e.length;r++)if(e[r].contentWindow===a.source){var i=a.data["datawrapper-height"][t]+"px";e[r].style.height=i}}}))}();
</script>
```

# Test web page with code

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

#install.packages("sentimentr")
library(tidyverse)
library(sentimentr)
library(tidyr)
```

# Example dataframe

```{r}
reviews <- tibble(
  id = 1:4,
  text = c(
    "The food was not good, but the service was extremely friendly.",
    "I barely enjoyed the movie, although the actors were talented.",
    "I am a vampire and I'm going to kill you and suck out your blood.",
    "I am excited that you are so happy."
  )
)
```

# 1. Split into sentences and calculate sentiment at the sentence level

```{r}
sentence_sentiment <- reviews %>%
  get_sentences() %>%
  sentiment_by(by = c("id")) # Summarizes back to row/document level if desired

```

```{r}
head(sentence_sentiment)
```
